rights_note: A US federal census schedule of 1900, in the public domain. Read for who lived at an address; no asset is derived from it.
access_notes: Read 2026-10-30 (T-3258) from the Internet Archive's page images; the item has no usable OCR (the schedules are handwritten). The enumeration districts were found by reading the street names written in each sheet's margin, not from an ED finding aid: the Steve Morse one-step ED tool returned nothing for a Prairie Avenue search. Readings marked with '?' in the reading table are the hand at its hardest; the cards say so where a name is affected.
note: The census asks for every person whose usual place of abode on 1 June 1900 was the dwelling, including live-in servants, which no society register prints. It is four years before the 1904 scene: what it supplies for 1904 is who kept a house in 1900, and the cards grade the servants and young children it names as inferred for that reason. Several Prairie Avenue families were away on the census day (in New Hampshire, at Highland Park, at Lakeside, in Europe); the enumerator wrote their names with the other columns blank and listed the servants who were in the house.
what_it_supplies: the live-in staff (cooks, maids, laundresses, nurses, butlers, coachmen and grooms) at the Prairie Avenue houses on 1 June 1900, by name, with birth month and year, birthplace, year of immigration and the work they did
the young children at home, whom the Blue Book never prints
the given names of wives and of daughters the Blue Book prints only as '& dr.'
which houses held a different family in 1900 from the one the 1904 Blue Book lists
what_it_does_not_supply: anything on 1 July 1904; a servant or child seen in 1900 is placed in the 1904 scene only by inference
the households the enumerators reached elsewhere (the Glessners at The Rocks, for one); their own entries were not searched
Prairie Avenue 1637, 1700, 1706, 1708 and 2001-2005, which were not found in the sheets read
the 1910 census, which was not read
